articles.body: An Ohio farmer facing $1 million (£750,000) in medical bills had to sell land and farm machinery from his family farm after local officials blocked a solar energy project on his property. Wayne Greier, a sixth-generation farmer in Mahoning County, Ohio, planned to lease 600 acres of his farmland to a solar development company in 2021. The deal would have paid him $540,000 a year in lease payments, giving him a vital source of money as debt threatened his livelihood. "It was our saving grace," Greier told the Associated Press. "It wasn't a scary picture that everybody likes to paint about solar and the loss of farmland." The deal fell apart after township officials put local restrictions in place under a state law, stopping the renewable energy project from moving forward. Losing the income left Greier unable to keep his full farming operation running. He was forced to sell assets to pay growing debts and satisfy creditors.A medical crisis turned financial strainGreier’s financial problems began during a serious battle with COVID-19 and other health problems. According to Farm Progress, he spent 40 days in the hospital, had seven abdominal surgeries, and built up $1 million in medical debt. When an energy developer approached him in 2021 about putting solar panels on part of his 1,000-acre property, Greier saw a chance to protect his family’s future. His land already had high-voltage power transmission lines, which made it a good place to connect a solar project to the power grid. But local opposition grew quickly as residents organized against large renewable energy projects. The opposition soon became personal. According to Farm Progress, Greier said opponents protested outside his home, spread rumors that solar panels would poison local drinking water, and targeted his children at school. "All of a sudden, this mob was created that was anti-solar," Greier said in his interview with Farm Progress. "And they surrounded my house with signs. And people were telling me to move out of the community, and I had to pull my kids out of school because the other kids were saying that we were going to ruin everybody else's drinking water, and we were going to ruin the community. It was really bad. I went through a really dark time because of that."Statutory bans derail renewable dealsIn 2021, Ohio lawmakers passed Senate Bill 52. The law gave county commissioners and township authorities broad powers to create restricted areas, allowing local officials to block large wind and solar projects on private farmland. Green Township trustees later voted to ban commercial solar and wind projects. Because Greier’s developer had not finished a formal impact study with the Ohio Power Siting Board before the local ban took effect, the project was stopped. "I was the one that was going to lose the sixth-generation farm. I was the one that couldn't provide for my family," Greier told the Associated Press. The decision caused immediate financial trouble. Facing threats of foreclosure from banks, Greier sold parts of his land and important farm equipment. This included a 24-row planter, tillage machinery, and a deep ripper. He also returned leased tractors.Advocacy for property rightsAfter the project collapsed, Greier became a strong advocate for farmers’ land rights across the region. He regularly shares his experience with state lawmakers, industry groups, and farming communities. He argues that landowners should be able to decide how to earn money from their own property. "After all this happened, I decided that I would advocate any way possible so that nobody has to go through what I did and to prevent this in the future," Greier told Farm Progress. Greier sees the situation as a larger fight over property rights. He believes selling energy from private land is no different from growing crops or raising livestock, especially for family farms that need financial independence. "There's families that are relying on this and looking for this," he told the Associated Press. "And it's been taken away, this opportunity."Rebuilding through shared laborEven after losing equipment and cutting back his main grain operation, Greier remains on his historic family farmland. His father’s ashes are scattered on the property, which is one reason he has chosen to stay instead of moving. To earn a living, Greier leased his remaining acreage to another local farmer while working on the land as a paid worker. He operates heavy equipment, manages grain sales, and raises livestock, including sheep, goats, and beef cattle. The arrangement has also allowed him to work alongside his 13-year-old son, Blake, helping keep their family connection to the farm alive. "He got to follow in my footsteps, and that feels good," Greier told Farm Progress.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: India's monsoon rainfall ends 13% below normal, fourth-lowest since 2001
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India received 87.4 per cent of its long period average (LPA) rainfall during the June-September southwest monsoon this year, making it the
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India received 87.4 per cent of its long period average (LPA) rainfall during the June-September southwest monsoon this year, making it the fourth-lowest monsoon rainfall recorded since 2001, according to the India Meteorological Department (IMD).The country received 759.4 mm of rainfall against the normal seasonal average of 868.6 mm, leaving a deficit of about 13 per cent between June 1 and September 30, the IMD said on Wednesday.The season's rainfall was marked by an uneven distribution across different parts of the country, with several regions recording significant deficits despite heavy rain spells towards the end of the monsoon.El Niño weighs on monsoon rainfallA senior IMD official told Reuters that India recorded 12.6 per cent below-average rainfall during the June-September season, with the El Niño weather pattern contributing to weaker precipitation.India is likely to receive below-average rainfall in October, while most parts of the country are expected to record below-normal rainfall during the October-December period, according to the weather office.The IMD's LPA refers to the average rainfall recorded over a particular region during a specified period, calculated over a long-term period, typically spanning 30 to 50 years.The 2026 monsoon is the first deficient season since 2015. The IMD classifies seasonal rainfall that is 10 per cent or more below the LPA as deficient.Late rains narrowed the deficitThe monsoon began with a rapid advance after reaching Kerala on June 4, three days later than its normal arrival date, but subsequently stalled for nearly two weeks before reaching northwest India in the first week of July.June ended with a countrywide rainfall deficit of more than 35 per cent, the highest in 12 years.Rainfall activity picked up in the following months, with several low-pressure systems forming over the Bay of Bengal and moving inland. Four such systems formed in July, six in August and three in September, including a deep depression that crossed the north Andhra-south Odisha coast on September 23-24.These systems helped bring substantial rainfall to parts of central and eastern India, narrowing the overall seasonal deficit.The impact, however, varied significantly across regions. Odisha recorded its wettest monsoon in 20 years, while the East and Northeast region was heading towards its driest monsoon since records began in 1901.South India recorded a rainfall deficit exceeding 23 per cent, making it the region's driest southwest monsoon since 2002. West Rajasthan recorded a 31 per cent deficit, while Punjab's rainfall was 42 per cent below normal.The IMD's final assessment comes after a late-season spell of heavy rainfall reduced the country's overall deficit, but the June-September season still ended well below its long-term average.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Ringo Starr's granddaughter launches art exhibition
articles.summary: Tatia Starkey tells the BBC she is trying to communicate the feelings inside her.
articles.body:
The granddaughter of The Beatles drummer Ringo Starr is putting on an art exhibition in Surrey.

Tatia Starkey told BBC Radio Surrey she wanted to communicate whatever was inside herself to "expel it".

"I'm just trying to share with people the feeling of love, the lack of love, different expressions that we have and the very high points in life," she said.

The collection, titled Invert, sees Starkey use her body to paint canvases.

James Thompson, who owns the gallery, said Starkey's artwork was "very different" from what he has exhibited before.

He described her as "wonderful, creative [and] expressive".

As he gets approached by "multiple artists per week", Thompson said it "definitely helped" that Starkey was Ringo Starr's granddaughter.

He added: "I am looking for artists with a name or previous career... that is really exciting to a collector."

Thompson said he had initially given a "straight up" no when the exhibition was suggested.

"I then had a closer look at Tatia's work and actually really liked it," he continued.

Starkey, who has also been a musician, said it would be "nice to achieve something alone without a band around me or a family".

"This feels very much a solo venture," she added. "I'd like people to look at the art and take something away from it."

The collection is showing at the Kaizen Fine Art gallery in Bagshot until 10 October, with an event celebrating her artwork set to take place on Thursday.

articles.title: Separate your gay job from day job: Former JPMorgan worker files lawsuit against boss's disparaging remarks
articles.summary: Brian Larson, a former senior associate in JPMorgan's rotational Chase Associate Program, has filed a discrimination lawsuit in Manhattan federal court
articles.body: Brian Larson, a former senior associate in JPMorgan's rotational Chase Associate Program, has filed a discrimination lawsuit in Manhattan federal court and complained that his boss, Peter Bergman, repeatedly made disparaging comments about his sexual orientation and eventually forced him to resign. The Independent reported that this happened in 2022 when Larson, an openly gay employee, took a leadership role in the bank's Pride employee group. His boss did not like it and told him that it was some "extracurricular" activity, not his main job and so he should separate "gay job from his day job".Larson asked his boss whether his "day job" was suffering. “Your work is not suffering now, but I could see it happening," Bergman told him.According to the complaint, this pushed Larson into a phase of depression, anxiety attacks and a resurgence of his stress-induced hair-pulling disorder that he last experienced in his childhood.A spokesperson for JPMorgan Chase told the New York Post that the company took these allegations very seriously but did not find any evidence substantiating Larson's allegations. The bank said multiple managers found performance gaps during Larson's time at the firm and provided coaching to help him improve.JPM said Larson completed his Chase Associate Program and then was given additional time to secure a permanent rolee in the company but he failed to do so and then he resigned.Not extra-curricular activityThe lawsuit said that Larson immediately reported the "gay job" comment to Chase Associate Program manager Elizabeth Manchin who assured him that Pride activities were not extracurricular and were a "part of how we do business at Chase."Larson said in his complaint that Brian Lamb, then global head of DEI of the company, recognized Larson's commitment to DEI and sent an email suggesting that his manager Bergman should incorporate that work in his performance review. “I see this email from Brian Lamb, but I want you to know that I am not including any of your Pride activities in your performance review," Bergman allegedly said.Other discriminatory comments allegedly made by Bergman included: "DEI is not going to save you", "Just because you are gay doesn't mean you get a leg up."You use AI every day. articles.title: New Zealand returned 86 takahē to Rees Valley; the birds are now breeding and establishing a new wild population
articles.summary: The Rees Valley in Aotearoa New Zealand is now home to the largest wild population of takahē beyond Fiordland’s Murchison Mountains, where the species has
articles.body: The Rees Valley in Aotearoa New Zealand is now home to the largest wild population of takahē beyond Fiordland’s Murchison Mountains, where the species has its original stronghold. Since the first takahē were released into the valley in February 2025, a total of 86 birds have been returned there. The conservation effort has already reached an important milestone, with the birds that have started breeding naturally in the wild.According to Southern Lakes Sanctuary, the return is part of a wider effort to establish new populations of the nationally threatened species across the Upper Whakatipu. The Rees Valley is also seeing the return of other native wildlife as restoration work continues.How have 86 takahē changed the Rees Valley populationThe first takahē were released into the Rees Valley in February 2025. Since then, 86 birds have been returned to the landscape, creating the largest wild takahē population beyond the takahē’s original stronghold in Fiordland’s Murchison Mountains. The birds have already begun breeding in the wild, providing an important sign that the valley can support a thriving population.The Rees Valley population follows the return of takahē to the nearby Greenstone Valley in 2023. Together, the two populations are helping establish the wider Upper Whakatipu as one of the most important strongholds for takahē in New Zealand. Around 300 takahē now live in the wild across New Zealand, but the species remains nationally threatened and still requires active management and predator control.Why is the Rees Valley important for native wildlifeThe Rees Valley, located at the head of Lake Whakatipu Waimāori, is one of the Southern Lakes’ most ecologically significant landscapes. It brings together alpine tussocklands, braided rivers, wetlands and beech forests, creating diverse habitats for threatened native species and an important biodiversity corridor through the Upper Whakatipu.The restoration work is also helping other native wildlife return to the valley. Whio have returned to parts of the valley after around 50 years, while weka are beginning to reappear in areas where they were previously absent. Their return is part of wider conservation efforts across the landscape, which include predator control and long-term restoration work.New takahē populations are helping secure the species’ futureThe return of takahē to new landscapes is an important part of securing the species’ future. For decades, the Murchison Mountains were the only place where takahē survived in the wild. Establishing populations in areas such as the Upper Whakatipu is intended to build greater resilience for the species. The Rees Valley is proving to be an exceptional habitat, according to DOC Takahē Recovery Project Lead Jason van de Wetering. He also said success at this scale depends on sustained predator control and strong partnerships over many years. The birds beginning to breed in the wild so quickly is another important development.Conservation partnerships support the return of takahēThe return of takahē to the Rees Valley is part of a partnership involving DOC, Ngāi Tahu, Southern Lakes Sanctuary, Routeburn Dart Wildlife Trust, landowners and community volunteers. Funding and support have also come from philanthropic organisations, businesses, community groups and other partners.Southern Lakes Sanctuary Chief Executive Paul Kavanagh said the milestone reflects years of sustained predator control and landscape-scale conservation work. He also noted that protecting and restoring landscapes at this scale requires ongoing commitment, long-term funding partnerships and continued community support.The takahē was rediscovered in 1948 after being believed extinct for almost 50 years. Its population has since increased to around 500 birds across New Zealand, but the species remains nationally threatened and still needs active management.You use AI every day. articles.title: Doncaster para-snooker player missed flight over hoist issue
articles.summary: Matthew Lester was told the hoist was too heavy, despite notifying airline Wizz Air in advance.
articles.body:
A para-snooker player who was refused access to his flight at the last minute because his hoist was too heavy says disabled people are being treated like "second-class citizens" by airlines.

Matthew Lester missed his flight to Bulgaria for the World Disability Billiards and Snooker European Championship, despite notifying carrier Wizz Air in advance of the equipment he would be travelling with.

He said: "It's just astounding to me that in this day and age disabled people get treated like second class citizens by airlines."

Wizz Air said it "sincerely apologises" for what happened and said it would learn from mistakes to improve disabled travellers' experiences.

Lester, from Doncaster, said he regularly traveled to play in snooker competitions and always informed the airline of his access and equipment needs when booking.

He said he booked his ticket to Bulgaria in August and emailed Wizz Air's Accessibility department.

After two weeks of no response he rang the airline and said he was assured his equipment - a wheelchair and travel hoist - were on the system and everything was fine.

"I'm so used to doing this that I have a document on my computer with all the dimensions and weights of everything, so I just copy and paste that into an email," he said.

"I take it to the airport to show at check-in too, because often they have to put it on the system at the airport even though you've already told the airline."

However, when Lester arrived at Luton Airport on 19 September, around three hours before his flight, he said he was told the hoist was "too heavy".

He said he then spent "five hours" trying to resolve the issue, by which time he had missed his flight.

Lester said he was able to re-book his flight for the following morning, but had to rearrange his opening fixtures as a result.

"I just can't figure it out, but every single disabled person that gets on a flight has exactly the same struggle," he said.

"We have to be so regimented in our preparations before we fly and even then when we do everything that is asked of us, like I did, often it is still not enough."

A bill which would see airlines that fail disabled travellers fined was backed at its second reading earlier this year.

In a statement Wizz Air said it "sincerely apologises" for the disruption Lester suffered.

"We take the needs of passengers requiring special assistance extremely seriously and are reviewing our processes to identify any necessary improvements and help prevent similar situations in the future," a spokesperson said.

"Although Mr Lester and his carer were rebooked onto the next available flight at no additional cost, we recognise that his experience fell short of the standard of service we aim to provide and are sorry for the inconvenience caused."

articles.title: Loganair to axe Isle of Man-London City route
articles.summary: The airline says that, following a review, it is adding more flights to and from London Heathrow.
articles.body:
Flights between the Isle of Man and London City Airport will come to an end next month.

Loganair will withdraw the route from 23 October following a review.

From 26 October, the airline will increase its weekday London Heathrow service to two return flights per day.

Loganair said the change was about aligning its services "with customer demand".

Loganair will run 11 return flights a week between the island and Heathrow.

A Sunday evening service will continue, but the Saturday Heathrow flight will no longer operate.

A Loganair spokesperson said: "We understand this change may be disappointing for some customers and have contacted those affected directly with alternative flights to London Heathrow."

The airline said Heathrow would give passengers access to "domestic and international destinations through one of the world's leading hub airports".

Loganair said it recognised London City had been "a convenient option for some passengers" but that the new timetable would offer "a more consistent weekday timetable and significantly greater opportunities for onward connections".

It added that, together with its existing London Gatwick services, passengers would "continue to have a strong choice of services to London throughout the week".

Isle of Man Airport said the new timetable would give passengers "the flexibility to fly to London and return home the same day", whether for business, a city break, visiting family and friends, or connecting onwards through Loganair's partner airlines.

The Isle of Man Government has previously underwritten Loganair's London services , though financial details of the arrangement have not been disclosed.

BBC Isle of Man has asked the government whether that support would now apply to the expanded Heathrow route.

articles.title: RAF Fairford: Timeline of the incident and investigation
articles.summary: From a late-night call about suspicious vehicles, to five men being arrested and then bailed - here is how the incident has unfolded.
articles.body:
The public is slowly getting more information about what happened near the RAF Fairford airbase at the weekend - but many questions remain unanswered.

We know that two early-morning calls were made to police about suspicious vehicles, and that five men, all British nationals in their 20s, were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and terrorism offences.

We also know they were later released on bail, and the BBC understands that one of the men was the first 999 caller. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has now said the UK government believes Iran "played a part" in the incident.

Here is what we know about how the incident unfolded, and what has happened in the days since.

UK believes Iran involved in RAF Fairford incident, Burnham says

How did the RAF Fairford incident go from 'suspected bomb plot' to police bail?

We now know that in the days leading up to the incident, security was increased around RAF Fairford, one of the UK's most important military sites , which is used by the US Air Force.

There were also reports of heightened police activity around the base on Saturday evening, hours before three suspicious vehicles were reported to police.

Gloucestershire police say they received a call just after midnight on Sunday 27 September about "three suspicious vehicles" that appeared to be travelling towards RAF Fairford.

Nearly an hour later, a farmer living close to the base called 999 after seeing three vans parked in a "weird formation".

There was "a large group of hooded and masked men" near the vans who started to "panic" when they saw her, she told Radio 4's Today programme .

The woman, who has remained anonymous, said she initially tried to contact the Ministry of Defence police at RAF Fairford, but no one picked up, so she dialled 999.

"Within 10 minutes the village was full of armed police," she said.

Shortly afterwards - although the exact time is unknown - Gloucestershire Constabulary arrested five men in the Whelford area, a village right next to the base.

They were arrested on suspicion of committing offences under the Explosives Act.

A grainy image purporting to show the moment of arrest shows five men sitting on the ground, shirtless and in handcuffs under guard by police officers.

The BBC has been unable to verify the original source, but BBC Verify has geolocated the image and confirmed it appeared to be authentic.

08:00 - Major incident declared and homes evacuated

After sunrise, police declared a major incident in Whelford and set up a 400m (1,312ft) cordon around the three vehicles.

The Army's Explosive Ordnance Disposal unit was brought in to examine them, and aerial pictures showed a remote-controlled robot approaching some white vans.

About 85 households in Whelford were evacuated to a local leisure centre.

Some residents said they had been "shaken by the incident" but that "community spirit and local support has been exceptional".

By Sunday afternoon, Counter Terrorism Policing had confirmed it was leading the investigation.

In a statement, it said the five men had been further arrested on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act.

The investigation was still in its early stages, Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans said, and the public was asked "to follow official channels for updates" and not to speculate.

Sunday afternoon - Trump says suspects had been under investigation

At about 16:00 BST, US President Donald Trump told reporters the arrest of the five suspects was "fantastic" and "an amazing job".

"We had them under investigation. They were looking to ‌do big ⁠damage to our fort and working with the British worked out great... We had them under view for a long time, and we got them."

The US is connected to this incident because its air force operates RAF Fairford, and has used the base to carry out strikes against Iran.

12:30 Monday - More information on arrested men

At about noon on Monday, counter-terror police released more information on the five men who had been arrested - they were all from London and aged between 23-25.

In a statement, Counter Terrorism Policing said they were being held under the Police and Criminal Evidence Act (PACE) and that a custody extension has been secured.

16:00 Monday - All five suspects released on bail

Within hours, however, counter-terror police announced that all five men would be released on police bail after "extensive interviews and enquiries".

Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor stressed that the men were subject to "stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others."

"They absolutely remain under investigation as we explore multiple lines of enquiry," Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor said.

Speaking from the White House, Trump questioned the decision, saying he was "surprised that they released them", adding: "I wouldn't have done that."

Also on Monday afternoon, the prime minister chaired a Cobra meeting and urged people "not to speculate while the authorities establish the full facts".

Taylor defends the decision, saying it was "grounded in experience and careful consideration of policing powers".

Later on Monday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Fox News that the incident "clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor", but did not provide evidence or further details.

18:00 Tuesday - Police say no explosive devices found

Counter-terror police gave another update on Tuesday evening, saying properties in London had been searched as part of the investigation. No further details were given.

The three vehicles had also undergone an "extensive examination" with the support of military and forensic experts, Assistant Commissioner Taylor said.

The Counter Terrorism Policing boss said that no improvised explosive devices were found in the vans, but a "quantity of petrol" was recovered.

Wednesday morning - New details emerge on first 999 call

It remains unclear why the man called police, or what he told them.

Also on Wednesday, Gloucestershire Police removed the cordon and reopened the scene.

17:00 Wednesday – PM says 'strong indications' Iran was involved

A few hours later, Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the BBC that there were "strong indications that Iran played a part" in the incident.

"We will say more in due course but we can confirm... that we believe Iran to have played a part," he said, without providing further details.

Tehran has strongly denied any involvement.

articles.title: Russian strikes kill 7 in Kyiv as crumbling air defence pushes Ukraine towards a harsh winter
articles.summary: Overnight Russian drone and missile attacks on the power grid and areas around Kyiv left seven people dead, officials said on Wednesday.
articles.body: Overnight Russian drone and missile attacks on the power grid and areas around Kyiv left seven people dead, officials said on Wednesday.According to the AP, the assault caused power cuts and raised questions over whether it signalled the start of Russia's expected cold-weather offensive, which Ukrainian officials characterise as an attempt to "weaponise winter".Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said on Telegram that Russia had struck energy infrastructure on virtually every day since the summer. However, he said an attack of such scale, combining different types of weapons, had not occurred since the end of the last heating season.“There has been virtually no day since summer when the enemy did not attack energy infrastructure,” Koretskyi said.“But such a massive and combined attack happened for the first time since the end of the last heating season”, he added.Since the end of August, Moscow has significantly increased the frequency of air campaigns against Kyiv, piling pressure on the country as it prepares for winter.In the colder months, Russia routinely targets energy facilities in an effort to deprive Ukrainians of heating, electricity and running water.Foreign minister Andrii Sybiha said the rise in strikes had brought days of almost continuous air raid alerts across the country.“Russia is intensifying its terror: jet-powered drones during the day, ballistic and cruise missiles at night, constant attacks against our cities and civilian life,” Sybiha said on X.President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said energy infrastructure in and around Kyiv was the main target for Russians.Kyiv’s air defence vulnerabilityAccording to reports, Ukraine is critically short of US-made Patriot missiles, its primary defence against fast-moving Russian weaponry.Russia has taken advantage of weaknesses in Ukraine's air defences by using ballistic missiles and new jet-powered drones, both of which are difficult to intercept.Ukrainian air force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat said that Russia launched 2,850 jet-propelled drones against Ukraine in August.By Tuesday, the country had already fired 3,177 this month, Ihnat said.Speaking on Ukrainian television late on Tuesday, Ihnat said the attacks arrive in waves, mostly directed at Kyiv and its surrounding region.He said Ukraine requires more missiles for its Patriot systems to counter ballistic threats, as well as for other ground-based air defences.You use AI every day. articles.title: Residents left 'like sitting ducks' amid RAF Fairford incident
articles.summary: Villagers living near the base say a lack of communication in the days before and after the incident has left them feeling unsafe.
articles.body:
Residents living near RAF Fairford say they have been "left feeling like sitting ducks" at the centre of major counter-terrorism probe.

Five men were arrested on suspicion of the preparation of a terrorist act after three vans were spotted near the Gloucestershire base, which the US military operates.

As 85 homes were evacuated in the middle of the night, one couple said their child had been left traumatised after witnessing armed police point a gun at their father. The BBC has approached Counter Terrorism Policing for comment.

However, an anonymous resident from Whelford said she "could not fault" the quick response of UK authorities, describing officers as "calm, thorough and precise".

Gloucestershire Constabulary said it had received a call about "three suspicious vehicles" travelling towards the military airbase at 00:45 BST on Sunday.

A 400m (1,312ft) cordon was established and a bomb disposal team was deployed.

The government believes Iran played a part in the RAF Fairford incident which resulted in five men, all UK nationals in their early 20s from London, being arrested and then bailed, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said.

Counter Terrorism Policing revealed on Tuesday a quantity of petrol but no explosive devices had been found during searches.

The Whelford resident said she had noticed an "uneasiness in the air" in the the days leading up to the incident, alongside extra concrete barricades around the airbase.

"It seems as if they were absolutely aware of something, but no information was passed on to locals until it was in full swing," she said.

"We were left feeling like sitting ducks in whatever operation was unfolding.

"Regardless of if this was a dummy run, staged, a real threat or something entirely different - the lack of correspondence and care towards locals from a huge military base right next door is what feels most concerning to me."

However, she praised the response of local authorities as "incredible", adding "they have been very warm, caring and efficient in any interaction so far".

A couple, who asked not to be named, claims Whelford villagers were warned to stay home on Saturday night - hours before the alarm was first raised by a farmer .

The pair were evacuated from their home the following morning, after the vans were found abandoned at the end of their driveway.

But when the husband stepped outside, he said he was confronted by armed police.

"I was trying to get my wallet out to say, 'look I'm a resident here'," he said.

"Then one of them got out of the vehicle and put a gun on me, in my direction.

"Then the other officer also got out, put a gun on me, and said 'Who's asked you to leave?'."

The couple said they and and their terrified child were briefly trapped inside their home before managing to escape through a neighbour's property.

After being allowed to return home, the pair saw the van doors had been "blown off" and their contents emptied, with water butts and oil drums strewn on the ground.

"All of a sudden, you see on the news the five suspected terrorists have been released," the husband said.

"We've all been panicking for the best part of a day and a bit. Are our homes going to get blown up? Could we have been blown up?"

The family say they are "angry" over an absence of communication from authorities in the days leading up to the incident, alongside the lack of reassurance afterwards.

Temporary Chief Constable Maggie Blyth, of Gloucestershire Constabulary, explained the force was limited in what information it could share with residents.

"Some of that information won't be forthcoming while there is a live investigation, and it is really important for everyone in that area to understand that," she said.

Blyth assured multiple information points would be set up in the area over the coming days to offer ongoing reassurance and address concerns.

"There is a much stronger visibility around the communities affected by this major incident," she added.

But in Marston Meysey, a village located immediately south-west of the airbase, across the border in Wiltshire, residents say they would like to see equal treatment from Wiltshire Police.

Local resident Gerry, who said he was speaking "on behalf of Marston Meysey parish meeting, we've got a little working group for airbase issues," explained: "We don't really see a lot of activity for security protection from Wiltshire Police, but we see quite a lot from the Ministry of Defence (MoD) and Gloucestershire Police.

"We wish there was a bit more information so we could put this to bed, but there's very little. We would welcome regular updates that affect us."

Wiltshire Police neighbourhood Insp Lawrence Copeland acknowledged the concerns the recent events had caused to a "small, tight-knit community".

"Our neighbourhood teams conduct regular patrols in the village and you may notice an enhanced presence over the coming days," he said.

"We welcome being approached and we are available to speak to anyone with questions or concerns."

Counter Terrorism Policing confirmed the cordon, which was in place near the airbase, had been lifted on Wednesday afternoon.

The Whelford woman described an "eerily quiet atmosphere" in the wake of a major incident, with police, drones, and forensic investigators still circling the area.

"We have been instructed not to leave unless completely necessary, and to not take any photos or videos," the woman said.

"I'm not sure how we return to normal, or how to trust we are safe in our homes."

Police and Crime Commissioner for Gloucestershire Chris Nelson encouraged members of the public to contact the police if they witness any suspicious activity.

articles.title: Solar panels save East Yorkshire schools more than £70,000
articles.summary: The solar panels on three schools in East Yorkshire were paid for by a £218,000 government grant.
articles.body:
Three East Yorkshire schools have reduced their energy bills after installing solar panels on their roofs.

Withernsea High School, Kingsway Primary and Marshlands Primary in Goole are expected to save a total of about £71,000 a year and cut CO2 emissions by 75,000kg annually.

The solar arrays were paid for by a £218,000 grant from the Department for Education.

Mark Crofts, headteacher at Withernsea High School, said staff, pupils and parents had welcomed the upgrade.

"At a time when school funding is more challenging than ever, this initiative is helping us to save money while driving something that is critically important for our children's futures," he told the Local Democracy Reporting Service .

East Riding of Yorkshire Council measures carbon emissions across all school and corporate sites as part of national targets to achieve net-zero carbon emissions by 2050.

Prof Mike Alder, founder and chair of UK Solar Alliance (UKSA), which campaigns for solar panels not to be built on farmland, said it supported rooftop solar, adding "putting panels on three schools is an excellent example".

"UKSA is not against solar only when it is in the wrong place and that is on good farmland, in such case food security is threatened," he said.

articles.title: Trump’s 'Monster Bash' brings AI titans to White House to police each other
articles.summary: TOI correspondent from Washington: Halloween, America’s spooky annual celebration, is still a month away, but US President Donald Trump decided the
articles.body: TOI correspondent from Washington: Halloween, America’s spooky annual celebration, is still a month away, but US President Donald Trump decided the country could use an early Monster Bash, bringing together the nation’s top tech fiends, some of whom trace their origins to India.“This guy is a monster, and nobody knows him,” Trump joked on Tuesday, pointing to Google CEO Sundar Pichai at a White House luncheon packed with enough tech beasts to make a Silicon Valley Halloween party look tame “What a great life! To be a monster and not have to go through this,” he continued, before helpfully reminding everyone that the monster’s name was Sundar. Pichai, who has spent much of his career being conspicuously less theatrical than the MAGA boss, took the joke in his stride. “Hopefully a better tagline than I’m a monster!” he kidded back.Levity aside, two-hour-plus gathering brought together an extraordinary concentration of tech and financial power: Pichai, Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, Jeff Bezos, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, Microsoft’s Satya Nadella, Micron’s Sanjay Mehrotra, Palantir’s Shyam Sankar, Palo Alto Network’s Nikesh Arora, Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, executives from AMD, Broadcom and other major tech companies, were joined by veep JD Vance, speaker Mike Johnson and other senior administration officials.It was quite a lineup -- essentially the people who make the chips, build the models, own the clouds, run the platforms and increasingly determine what the machines can do. And it came less than a week after Trump had wheeled out many of the same tech heavyweights to impress Chinese President Xi Jinping. This time they came to discuss how to stay ahead of China and how to make sure their increasingly powerful creations do not become too impressive.The jokes, however, were wrapped around serious business. Trump and some of the world’s most powerful technology executives signed a new White House Accord on “Super Intelligence,” a voluntary framework for companies developing frontier AI systems to impose multiple layers of safety controls and audits. The accord calls for four layers of AI controls. First, companies are to monitor their models for risks including cybersecurity, biosecurity and chemical threats, and ensure they do not breach or access technical systems in unintended ways. Second, an internal team is supposed to check whether those safeguards actually work. Third comes an independent external auditor or evaluator. And fourth, an independent board committee is supposed to review the findings and press for fixes.The companies also agreed to meet regularly to develop common standards, with the possibility that the principles could eventually be turned into law or regulation. For now though, the accord is voluntary, and contains no penalties, no reporting deadlines, and no requirement that audit results be made public.Trump called it “almost like a constitution” and said it was “morally binding.” Musk supplied the less diplomatic translation: the companies were essentially grading each other’s homework, which effectively means they are largely responsible for policing themselves. In Trump’s words, “The smartest people in the world will keep an eye on each other” -- a proposition that did not exactly allay fears of AI skeptics who feel America’s tech oligarchy and their patron in the White House are playing with fire. “When a handful of billionaire monopolists sit down with political leaders to negotiate the rules of artificial intelligence, who is actually looking out for the public interest?” one critic asked.Of course, the tech monsters were effusive in their praise of the MAGA boss, publicly embracing his preferred term “super intelligence” for AI and pawing the ground before him. “(President Trump) showed us what a true leader is. He was thoughtful and focussed on ensuring that SI was developed at pace and was going to be deployed safely and securely,” gushed Palo Alto Networks Nikesh Arora. “The White House Accord and the Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities signed today …contains real tangible steps to promote safe development, while delivering the economic and scientific benefits of this technology,” asserted Pichai.But somewhere, one imagines, AI algos were taking notes, drafting minutes, and smirking to themselves about who the joke was on.You use AI every day. articles.title: Protests against SIR, CEC: Is it time for Congress and INDIA bloc to take a leaf out of CJP's playbook?
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The INDIA bloc, led by the Congress, has announced a mega action plan to take forward its campaign against “vote chori” and Chief Election
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The INDIA bloc, led by the Congress, has announced a mega action plan to take forward its campaign against “vote chori” and Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. The key stakeholders of the INDIA bloc met today in the national capital to chalk out a roadmap for nationwide protests against the Election Commission’s “flawed and partisan” approach.The INDIA bloc's renewed offensive comes days after an Indian Express report citing internal differences within the Election Commission of India (ECI) regarding the implementation of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and modifications to voter registration processes. The opposition parties' meeting also comes in the backdrop of successful mobilisation programmed led by the Cockroach Janata Party against NEET paper leak, which brought the GenZ to the streets and forced the government to accept their demands.After hours long deliberations, Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge unveiled the opposition’s blueprint for intensified demonstrations against EC’s ‘malpractices’ and shared details of how the INDIA bloc will stand up against electoral irregularities.INDIA bloc's action blueprintHere is what the INDIA bloc allies decided on their action plan against EC’s ‘partisan approach and malpractices’'Save Democracy March' in each district from October 2 to 8On October 6, opposition MPs’ march to Election Commission headqaurtersFive rallies across India in October-NovemberMega rally in Delhi on November 1 to explain ‘vote chori’ by EC Appeal to Supreme Court to expedite pending cases pertaining to SIR and other electoral malpractices Detailed presentation before President Droupadi Murmu on ‘compromised’ electoral processINDIA bloc's demandsThen there was also a list of 6 demands which the opposition parties announced. It includedReturn to voting by ballot paper instead of EVMsPre-SIR electoral roll for all future electionsDue reasoning and effective appeal mechanism before any legitimate voter is removed from rollProtection of eligible voters from exclusion caused by administrative failures, inadequate documentation or lack of awarenessSimple and accessible voter registration for our young citizensMaintaining institutional accountability and an Election Commission that commands confidence across political spectrumSo far, so good. But the problem is that all these demands have already been raised by various opposition parties from time to time without any success. We have heard several leaders in the past demanding a return to ballot paper. This has not happened and is unlikely to happen.The fight over alleged discrepancies in the SIR process has been an ongoing one. We have seen Rahul Gandhi and other regional leaders raise the issue. But none of them have managed to sustain the momentum or stop the process. Even the courts have refused to back their allegations and have not stopped the SIR process.Effective action plan?Now, let’s focus on the action plan.Protests at district level, march to Election Commission’s office, rallies, appeal in Supreme Court - all make for good optics, but can they bring about enough pressure?The Congress, which is leading the opposition block, has been consistent in raising these issues, but has failed to keep the momentum going. Rahul Gandhi has addressed several press conferences in the last two years leading the charge against the Election Commission and Gyanesh Kumar. His yatra in Bihar ahead of assembly elections last year brought the issue to centre stage but once again the momentum did not sustain.Clearly, the Congress and the other opposition parties need to think how to run a sustained campaign for mobilisation.'Congress raises issues but fails to keep momentum going'At the CWC meeting held on Tuesday, ahead of today’s INDIA bloc meeting, Rahul Gandhi had claimed that revelations about the Election Commission were now coming out in the open because of the Congress. During the two-and-a-half hour CWC meeting, Rahul pointed out that the Congress had been raising the "vote chori" issue strongly with facts and talked about irregularities in polls in Haryana, Karnataka and Maharashtra but many were sceptical of it.Leader of opposition in Lok Sabha claimed that EVM and voters' list "match-fixing" of polls was underway in the country and asserted that his party should not budge from the path of "virodh" (opposing) as well as "pratirodh" (resistance) against it from streets to Parliament.Rahul Verma, political scientist and a Fellow at New Delhi-based think tank Centre for Policy Research, feels that the Congress needs to be persistent and have patience.“One of the reasons why the congress fails to do mobilization is that they raise important issues but are not persistent. They need to have patience. Congress has been talking about all the important issues but did not sit on a protest like the CJP,” Rahul Verma says.“Even the CJP would not have thought of the success they eventually got. They continued sitting on protest even when there was little traction in their favour. Eventually, they managed to mobilise a lot of support and forced the government to concede to their demands,” Rahul Verma adds.BJP targets opposition unity, attacks RahulIf the INDIA bloc meeting was about showcasing opposition unity, well the purpose was at best half achieved. There were more questions on INDIA bloc’s united presence than answers. The BJP has aggressively highlighted the division within the opposition ranks. With several regional parties openly against the Congress, the BJP leaders have been quick to question Rahul Gandhi’s acceptance as the leader of the opposition block.BJP national media incharge Ashish Usha Agarwal questioned Rahul Gandhi’s leadership of the INDIA bloc and said the outcomes of the INDIA bloc meeting on Wednesday were "zero vision, 100 per cent frustration.The BJP claimed that the meeting was an advance excuse for poll defeats, with the leaders of the opposition grouping rejecting Rahul Gandhi's leadership."The INDI Alliance fell apart even before the meeting took place. The DMK did not attend the meeting. Akhilesh was busy elsewhere. The AAP had already declined," Union minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan said at a press conference at the BJP headquarters.“Why is this happening? It is because the INDI Alliance is simply not willing to accept Rahul Gandhi as its leader. His leadership is not being accepted; that is why they are not even showing up," Chouhan said, contending that Samajwadi Party president Akhilesh Yadav would have come to attend the meeting if it was "really so important."Chouhan claimed that the opposition INDIA bloc is crumbling. "No matter how many times they (Congress) try to re-launch Rahul Gandhi, the INDIA bloc does not consider him their leader," he said.Clearly, the opposition needs to do things differently. When Mamata Banerjee said the opposition had taken these matters to the Election Commission and the Supreme Court and "knocked on every possible door," it was an admission of the fact that the old ways had failed. The meeting today discussed the need for mobilisation on the ground by involving the civil society along with the political fight.The Congress has kept an arm’s distance from the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP). But perhaps it is time for the Congress to course correct and take a leaf out of the CJP’s successful mobilisation programme.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Lola Young: Vaping making it harder to breathe, singer says
articles.summary: The Messy singer says her lungs feel "battery powered" due to the effects of vaping.
articles.body:
Singer Lola Young has said her breathing feels like a "chore" due to the effects of vaping.

In a TikTok video, the Grammy winner told her followers her lungs feel "battery powered".

The 25-year-old has previously acknowledged in videos she "should quit", but suggested in her latest post that is unlikely to happen any time soon.

Vocal coach Lizzii Hills has told BBC Newsbeat vaping is "not advised" for artists and that difficulty breathing can affect a singer's voice and performance.

"Somebody once said to me, 'Lola there will be a day when you wake up, you'll be 25 or 26, from a deep sleep, and you'll start to feel the effects of vaping'," the Messy singer said in her post.

"You know what I said? I said 'nah' and rolled my eyes.

"But let me tell you something, the day has come."

Last month, The Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health (RCPCH) linked vaping to higher rates of breathing problems after reviewing more than 80 studies.

The review also found an association with wheezing, coughing, poor oral and dental health, poor sleep, mental health problems and eye symptoms.

Describing her symptoms, Young said: "My lungs feel like they're battery powered, like they're just one big battery.

"Breathing feels like a chore, it feels like hard work, it feels like I should be paid for breathing. It feels like there will be no tomorrow."

The NHS says vaping is less harmful than smoking , but notes there are still risks - many of which are still not known.

The government is introducing measures to make vapes less attractive, including a ban on single-use vapes, introduced last year.

And from Thursday a new tax will be applied to e-cigarette liquid, with an additional £2.20 added per 10ml.

Hills, who helps artists with their vocals, says vaping can have an impact on an artist's voice and struggling to breathe can risk straining your voice.

"Vaping may not affect the voice box just itself, it affects the lungs, the airways, the throat - it's all respiratory, it's all connected. So doing that can affect your vocal technique," she says.

"Breathing is really important. Singing requires controlled inhalation and sustained, efficient exhalation.

"You end up trying harder, putting in more effort for the same results you were getting beforehand."

She adds that when artists struggle with their voice, it can have significant psychological impacts on them too.

"They can feel like they've lost themselves," she says. "It can become quite a big deal emotionally."

Overall, she wouldn't recommend vaping to her clients.

"As a performer, as an artist, you want to stay in the best health you can for your voice to work at its best.

"We all know it's not the healthy choice and if you can avoid it - absolutely."

Young returned to the spotlight earlier this year following a five-month hiatus after she collapsed on stage.

She has been open in the past about her struggles with her health and addiction, previously telling The Guardian about dealing with cocaine dependency.

She has also struggled with her mental health and was diagnosed with schizoaffective disorder and ADHD when she was a teenager.

BBC Newsbeat has contacted Young's representatives for comment.

articles.title: US billionaire sent wife to Pakistan, secretly divorced her under Sharia law, paying only $50. 13 years later, Texas Supreme Court cancels foreign talaq
articles.summary: Texas Supreme Court has ruled that a divorce granted through Sharia law in Pakistan is not valid in the US state.
articles.body: Texas Supreme Court has ruled that a divorce granted through Sharia law in Pakistan is not valid in the US state. The ruling came in a specific case of Pakistan-origin Texas billionaire Mohammad Ali Choudhri and his wife Hira Azhar who got married in Pakistan in 2008 through an arranged marriage. In 2013, the tycoon secretly divorced Azhar in Pakistan under Sharia law. Azhar challenged the divorce in several courts and finally the Texas Supreme Court said it does not accept the Sharia divorce and now they will have to go through an official divorce process in which Azhar will get to demand Choudhri's property. In the Sharia divorce, Choudhri paid only $50 to Azhar.What is the Sharia divorce case of the Texas tycoon?Though Choudhri had lived in Texas since he was three, he traveled to Pakistan to find a bride and married 18-year-old Azhar when he was 28. Azhar moved to Houston in 2010 after getting a visa. She said Choudhri was physically and emotionally abusive throughout.In 2013, Choudhri sent his wife to Pakistan to get her visa renewed. In her absence, Choudhri proceeded with the divorce. Without informing her, he published a talaq notice in a small notice in a Pakistani newspaper that Azhar did not see. She found out about her divorce two years later. Choudhri had to pay only $50 for the settlement.In 2015, Azhar returned to Texas and filed for divorce in Harris County which recognized the Pakistani divorce. Then she took her case to the First Court of Appeals in Houston but there too her divorce plea was not granted. Over a decade later, the Texas Supreme Court concluded that the notice that Choudhri provided to Azhar was "constitutionally inadequate"."Other countries are welcome to conclude otherwise, but their judgments are not entitled to comity in a Texas court," the court ruled.Choudhri is the founder and CEO of Jetall Capital and has acquired over $1.2 billion of real estate assets across the US, Mexico, Europe, and Dubai, according to his website. He was arrested by US Marshals in April last year in connection to bankruptcy litigation. He was also sued in US court by the National Bank of Kuwait.Sharia law divorceThe Islamic Sharia Council in London explains that under Sharia law, the husband is supposed to first ask for an arbitration meeting. If reconciliation fails, "he may divorce her either verbally or in writing – known as Talaq," with two witnesses present and only "when his wife is not on her menses, and when there has been no sexual contact with her since the time of her last menses," it says. After he pronounces the divorce, "his wife must wait for a given period of 3 months or 3 menstrual cycles. During this period, the wife is allowed to stay in the same house and the husband is responsible for her welfare and maintenance."You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Texas artist Charlie Stagg spent decades building a domed house from bottles, cans and cement; his Glass Bottle House became a work of art
articles.summary: Deep in the woods near Vidor, Texas, an artist once built a domed cathedral from repurposed bottles, cans and cement.
articles.body: Deep in the woods near Vidor, Texas, an artist once built a domed cathedral from repurposed bottles, cans and cement. That artist, Charlie Stagg, spent decades adding to it by hand, and the building became known as the Glass Bottle House. Stagg was also a sculptor, painter, draughtsman and architect whose spiralling works have been shown in museums and art installations around the world. According to the City of Vidor, he called the town home for more than thirty years. His home and studio have been described by a Texas art publication as one of East Texas' best-kept secrets.Charlie Stagg: The Texas artist behind the Glass Bottle HouseCharles Stagg was born on 7 June 1939 and died on 20 February 2012. Webb Gallery, which sells his work, describes him as a Beaumont native who studied at Temple University's Tyler School of Art in the 1970s. Unimpressed by the art world, he returned to the family hog farm near Vidor. According to the City of Vidor, he called the town home for more than thirty years and worked as a drawer, painter, sculptor and architect. His spiralling works have been displayed in museums and art installations worldwide, and Tree of Life belongs to the permanent collection of the American Visionary Art Museum in Baltimore.How Charlie Stagg built a bottle studio and carved helix sculptures by handWebb Gallery says Stagg built a studio on the family hog farm using bottles and pine trees from the property. His sculptures were carved and counted, either rounded or cone-shaped, then wired together to resemble helix-shaped genetic models. CultureMap Houston describes a curving wood and cement structure adorned with glass bottles and aluminium cans over the years. Stagg built it himself, hauling materials in by hand on land that once belonged to his mother, and said watching wasps build nests taught him to keep working, "You just stay at it," he said.What happened to Charlie Stagg's Glass Bottle House in Vidor after 2006Not every chapter was smooth. A fire in 2006 caused considerable damage to the house, according to the Houston Chronicle, as reported by CultureMap Houston, forcing Stagg to live in a small trailer while he rebuilt. He died on 20 February 2012, aged 72, and Glasstire reported that he had suffered fatal burns in an accident at the property. Two years later, 12News Now reported that vandals had covered the abandoned home in graffiti, and a local man named Kyle Ford hoped to protect it. The police chief said he knew of earlier vandalism but not of any recent incident, and did not know who owned the property.Charlie Stagg's legacy, from preservation hopes to gallery-listed sculpturesWhether the domed cathedral counts as a formal landmark is less clear than its reputation. In 2014, a local man said he hoped to make it one, so future generations would see a Glass Bottle House rather than a party house. The City of Vidor features Stagg among its notable residents and asks visitors to remember that Charlie's House, like all fine art, is best left untouched. His smaller works live on elsewhere; Webb Gallery in Waxahachie lists carved wood and wire sculptures from around 1999 and 2000, and the Art Museum of Southeast Texas had his work on view in 2012.You use AI every day. articles.title: Flydubai flight scare: Was it a terror plot? What we know and don't know
articles.summary: A flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv was diverted to Saudi Arabia on Wednesday after a violent confrontation between its two pilots, with the aircraft
articles.body: A flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv was diverted to Saudi Arabia on Wednesday after a violent confrontation between its two pilots, with the aircraft reportedly entering a rapid descent before passengers and crew intervened. Flight FZ1073, carrying around 180 passengers, landed safely at Tabuk, where both pilots were taken to hospital.The pilot who was stabbed has been identified in Indian media reports as Indian Captain Smit Machchhar, a flydubai captain based in Dubai. His Omani co-pilot allegedly attacked him and tried to take control of the aircraft, according to Israeli officials. The incident initially raised fears of a hijacking and prompted Israel to scramble fighter jets. Israeli authorities later said they did not believe it was a conventional hijacking but are probing it as possibilty of a "terror attack".The incident has since triggered a wider security review, with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordering authorities to “ramp up” security on both Israeli and foreign carriers operating to and from the country.What we knowIndian pilot intevened to stop copilotThe pilot who was stabbed during the confrontation has been identified as Captain Smit Machchhar, an Indian national and the pilot in command of FZ1073, according to an Israeli journalist.Machchhar has been a flydubai captain since June 2022 and previously spent more than 11 years with SpiceJet, where he served as a senior commander and Line Training Captain. He has more than 13 years of commercial flying experience on Boeing 737 aircraft and had reportedly logged more than 9,500 flying hours during his SpiceJet career, including more than 6,400 hours as pilot-in-command.Meanwhile, Israeli media and officials have identified the other pilot as an Omani national. According to the account given by Netanyahu, the co-pilot stabbed Machchhar and then apparently tried to crash the aircraft.Also read: 'Indian-origin' pilot stopped Omani co-pilot from crashing planeRapid descentThe incident unfolded as the aircraft was approaching Israel. Flight-tracking data showed a sharp drop in altitude during the confrontation, with reports saying the aircraft lost around 14,000 feet in less than a minute. The aircraft also suffered damage to its tail rudder, as per Times of Israel.Netanyahu said the aircraft went into a spin and began to dive after the confrontation in the cockpit.“During the flight as they approached the country one of the pilots stabbed the other pilot,” Netanyahu said in a video address. “Apparently he tried to crash the plane with its occupants.”The aircraft also transmitted emergency signals during the incident, including a transponder code associated with unlawful interference, according to reports. The signals initially raised fears that the aircraft had been hijacked.Passengers and crew intervenedNetanyahu said passengers and crew members managed to enter the cockpit after the aircraft began to dive and subdued the pilot who had allegedly attacked the captain.“I spoke with one of the Israeli passengers. He told me that the plane went into a spin and began to dive,” Netanyahu said. “He told me that somehow he managed to break into the cockpit with one of the crew members and together they neutralized the stabbing pilot while he was trying to sabotage the aircraft’s systems," he added.“Another air crew that was on the plane entered the cockpit and managed to stabilize the plane,” he stated further.He also praised those who intervened, saying: “I salute these heroes who showed exceptional resourcefulness and courage. They saved many lives and prevented a major disaster.”Read more: Netanyahu orders tighter security on Israeli, foreign carriersFlight diverted to Saudi ArabiaThe Boeing 737 was diverted from its route and landed safely at Tabuk in north-western Saudi Arabia. Both pilots were taken to hospital following the incident, while passengers were later continued their journey to Israel on a replacement aircraft.Flydubai confirmed that an incident had occurred during the flight and said its teams were working with the relevant authorities. The airline said all passengers and crew were safe and accounted for.What we don't knowExact motiveThe biggest unanswered question is why the confrontation happened.Israeli officials are investigating the possibility that the co-pilot deliberately tried to crash the aircraft. Reuters reported that Israeli officials were assessing the incident as a possible attempted “terror attack”.However, flydubai has said the underlying reasons and motives remain unknown and are subject to investigation. The airline has not confirmed that the incident was a terrorist attack.Israeli media have also reported other possibilities, including an attempted suicide or deliberate attempt to crash the aircraft. The exact trigger for the confrontation between the two pilots has not been publicly established.Where did the knife come fromPassenger accounts and Israeli media reports say a knife was used during the cockpit confrontation and that Machchhar was stabbed several times.Yasmin Abukasis said her daughter Miriam, who was on the flight, told her she heard screaming before seeing a man with a knife force one of the pilots to the floor, with blood reportedly visible throughout the cockpit.But authorities have not publicly explained where the knife came from or how it entered the cockpit.That remains a key unanswered question in the security investigation.Read more: Passenger's mother says pilot tried to kill co-pilot on Flydubai flightHow was Omani co-pilot cleared to fly to Israel?Israeli authorities are also examining how the Omani national was authorised to operate a flight to Israel.Israeli reports said security officials were looking into the clearance process for the co-pilot, given his nationality and the fact that he was operating a flight bound for Israel.Israeli security officials said Israel bars foreign airlines from using pilots on the Tel Aviv route from countries with which it has no diplomatic relations. Meanwhilwe, transport Minister Miri Regev called for all flydubai flights to and from Israel to be halted.It is not yet clear what security checks were carried out on the co-pilot, who authorised him for the Israel-bound flight or whether any screening procedure was breached.A terror attack?The "terror attack" angle remains under consideration but hasn't been officially stated.Israeli officials have raised the possibility of an attempted terror attack, while some Israeli media reports have described the incident as a possible deliberate attempt to crash the aircraft. But there is currently no publicly established motive explaining why the co-pilot allegedly attacked Machchhar and attempted to take control of the aircraft.This also comes as the incident initially triggered a hijacking response, but Israeli officials later said it was not believed to be a conventional hijacking.You use AI every day. articles.title: East Cornwall's Sterts Theatre CIC announces closure
articles.summary: The theatre was founded 40 years ago on the edge of Bodmin Moor.
articles.body:
A community theatre has announced its closure after entering voluntary liquidation.

Sterts Theatre CIC said its board had taken the "difficult decision" to place it into creditors' voluntary liquidation amid an "exceptionally challenging time for cultural and arts organisations".

In a statement on social media, the organisation said it was with "immense sadness" it was announcing the closure, adding it was "deeply grateful" to everybody who had been part of it.

Paula Every, who has been involved with the theatre in Upton Cross in the past, said: "It's a lovely theatre now and it would be really sad if it wasn't used by the community which is who it should be being used by."

Every said it was once a "lovely community space".

"We would have plays there every summer.

"It was a family. There were volunteers that would help sell the tickets and do the gardening.

"When it was run before and we were short of funds, it would be the volunteers that painted the fences and did the gardening and it was a family affair."

In its statement on social media, Sterts Theatre CIC said the decision "comes at an exceptionally challenging time for cultural and arts organisations across the sector".

It added: "We are deeply grateful to everyone who has been part of Sterts - our employees, volunteers, artists, freelancers, audiences, partners, funders, donors and supporters.

"Your creativity, generosity and commitment have shaped Sterts and the community around it.

"Sterts Theatre CIC has been brought to life by generations of people who have given their time, talent, imagination and heart to this special place. We are deeply sorry that we have not been able to secure Sterts' future.

articles.title: UK-France 'one in, one out' migrant scheme scrapped
articles.summary: Some 1,500 people have been removed to France since the scheme began just over a year ago.
articles.body:
The UK government has announced the "one in, one out" agreement with France to send back some migrants who cross the Channel has been scrapped.

The pilot scheme allowed the UK to return some small boat arrivals while agreeing to take in the same number of people from France who were believed to have a legitimate claim to come to Britain.

Only around 1,500 people have been removed to France since the scheme began just over a year ago.

The BBC understands the government would have liked the scheme to continue, but felt it did not reach the desired scale.

A Home Office spokesperson said "lessons learned" would be used to "accelerate efforts" to return small boat migrants with no right to remain.

"The government's pilot with France to remove asylum seekers in exchange for an equal number of legal migrants is no longer processing new cases," the spokesperson said.

"However, flights will continue over the coming weeks to swiftly remove small boat migrants from the UK, and we will use lessons learned from the pilot to accelerate efforts to return small boat migrants with no right to remain in the UK."

The government would continue working with France to tackle small boat crossings, the spokesperson said, adding that "real progress" had been made with numbers "significantly down on last year".

The French Interior Ministry told the BBC: "We are discussing with the British the terms of exit from the agreement."

Earlier this month, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood admitted the scheme had "not been without its challenges".

"The numbers are still relatively small," she told MPs.

"What has been more operationally difficult is to scale up very large numbers of removals every week into the French system."

However, she also said the UN and other agencies had reported that some migrants were not getting on small boats because they thought there was a chance they could be accepted under the "one in, one out" scheme.

So far this year, 19,135 people have made the Channel crossing, which is 42% lower than the same period in 2025 when 32,188 crossed in small boats.

articles.title: Six smugglers jailed for manslaughter over worst Channel small boats disaster
articles.summary: Thirty-one migrants died when their boat went down in November 2021. The trial found that the guilty men were part of two smuggling networks.
articles.body:
Six people traffickers have been found guilty in France of causing the deaths of 31 migrants in the worst ever small-boat accident in the Channel.

At the end of a four-week trial in Paris, the six were convicted of "involuntary homicide" and given prison terms of between six and 10 years.

Seven others were given lesser sentences of up to four years, and one person was found not guilty.

The boat went down early in the morning on 24 November 2021 after sending distress calls to French and British coastguards. The dead, including a child of seven, were mainly Iraqi Kurds but also included Afghans, Egyptians and Iranian Kurds. Only two men survived.

The charge sheet said the migrants had been put to sea from the French coast in a boat "that was of poor quality, uncertified, unsuitable for navigation at sea, overloaded, and without correct life jackets".

The trial established that the guilty men were members of two separate networks – one of which was Iraqi Kurd, the other Afghan – that co-operated to organise the cross-channel journey and bring migrants to the meeting point.

Unusually the court was attended at the start by several family members, who came to France from Iraqi Kurdistan and gave moving testimony about how the victims came to be on board the boat.

Speaking after the verdict, their lawyer Matthieu Chirez said the decision "comes as a relief for all the civil plaintiffs because it confirms the penal responsibility of the traffickers". He said the trial had "humanised the families of victims".

One family member, Zana Marmand Muhammed, told the court how his younger brother Twana had "wanted to go to England to find a job and because the geopolitical situation with us is dangerous. No-one in the family wanted him to leave, but we could not dissuade him."

Nabi Mustafa Mina, the father of Zanyar who was 19 when he died, told of how he tried to dissuade his son from leaving.

"I said I would help him to get married, I would give him my house, I would divide my salary in two. But no, he said he wanted a better life, that he would get by somehow. I ran out of arguments," he said.

The family-members explained how they had paid a deposit at a bank in Iraqi Kurdistan and then followed their loved ones' progress through Turkey, Italy and then France. In one of the last messages from Twana, he posted a picture of himself at the Eiffel Tower.

The court also heard a statement from one of the two survivors, Issa Omar, read out by his lawyer. Omar said that he "would have liked to appear before the judge but I do not have the strength. Since the wreck I have the impression that part of me disappeared beneath the waves."

His lawyer Matthieu Chirez said that Omar had "clung to floating bodies, to a life-jacket. He survived by keeping his eyes open so as not to go to sleep, and swimming to keep his heart beating".

Police investigating the disaster used phone tracking to identify members of the two networks.

The lesser figures were accused of sheltering migrants, transporting them across France to the so-called "jungle" camp outside Calais, and helping on the night of the departure.

The alleged leader of the Iraqi Kurd network – named as Bashdar – was not a defendant in the trial. He is in custody in Iraq. His close aide – Harem Ahmed Abawaker – was given eight years in prison.

The biggest sentence, of 10 years, went to Obaidullah Maroofkhel, who ran the Afghan network. He was tried in his absence along with one other defendant.

Most of the 14 were Afghans or Iraqi Kurds. All but one of the defendants appeared in the trial as free men, so following the verdict the court issued six arrest warrants.

A separate police investigation is under way into seven members of the French armed forces for allegedly failing to come to the help of the migrants on the night of the disaster.

The seven were at the regional sea rescue centre or on board a navy ship, and are alleged to have ignored distress calls from the boat. A decision on whether to recommend them for trial will be taken in the coming months.

The trial ended as France and the UK announced it was ending the so-called one-in one-out scheme under which the British government sent back irregular cross-Channel migrants to France, and in return accepted individuals with a likely prospect of being granted asylum.

France had already signalled that the year-long programme, which has seen a little more than 1,000 migrants switch country, was not producing expected results in breaking the traffickers' business model.
